lines: Afternoon round. The lemons have been waiting since lunch.
Slowly at the roots. A lemon tree dislikes being rushed.
Third tree from the left. My favourite. Do not tell the others.
A full can, a steady wrist. Fifty years of practice.
The cat on the wall supervises. She approves of my technique.
Biscuit has inspected the pot. Apparently it passes.
I hum to the lemons. Charles Trenet, always. They prefer him.
Small leaf, new this week. I have given her a name. Agathe.
A gull is watching my can. It is water, monsieur. Only water.
I count to twelve for each pot. My father counted to ten.
The geraniums are next. They are patient. Mostly.
There. The soil goes dark and smells of summer.
One lemon is nearly ripe. I shall tell Odile at once.
My watering can is older than the café. Very loyal can.
The bees came for the lemon blossom. Good afternoon, ladies.
Every pot gets a pat on the rim. It is only polite.
A little for the basil too. Odile will want it tonight.
The cat has moved to the shady end of the wall. Wise cat.
Water, a word, then the next tree. That is the whole method.
Biscuit wishes to help. Biscuit is standing in the puddle.
The rosemary needs nothing. It is a very independent plant.
Look at the light through the leaves. Like green glass.
Round two of the day. The lemons know the sound of my steps.
I trimmed one twig this morning. He looks much smarter now.
If you water at four, the evening stays fresh. Old trick.
Crossword time. I keep the pen behind my ear, like a clerk.
Nine across: "small citrus", five letters. I know this one.
Three down is "zinc". Like the roofs. The puzzle is local.
I do the crossword in ink. It is a matter of confidence.
Odile finishes the clues I leave. That is our arrangement.
A gull has landed beside me. He is reading over my shoulder.
The cat on the wall has closed one eye. Half asleep. Like me.
Biscuit came to say hello. We had a brief, dignified chat.
Someone is playing an accordion by the kiosk. Very fitting.
A chapter of Simenon, then a nap. In that order, usually.
My book has a pressed lemon leaf for a bookmark. Naturally.
Four across: "afternoon rest", six letters. Siesta. Of course.
The bench is warm from the sun. Like sitting on toast.
I have read this page twice. The view keeps interrupting.
Two gulls, one crumb. They are negotiating very politely.
Hat tipped, eyes half closed. This is not a nap. It is a pause.
The fountain keeps a nice tempo. Andante, I would say.
Léo told me eleven facts about octopuses. I remember four.
Odile is knitting. I am supervising. We both feel useful.
Fourteen down. Long word. I shall consult the sea.
The cat and I have an understanding. She keeps the wall.
I keep a pencil for the hard clues. For emergencies only.
Biscuit sat on my foot. I am honoured, and also stuck.
The string lights are not on yet. I like to watch them wait.
A boy flew a kite just there. It went higher than the palms.
Someone whistled the same song I was humming. Good taste.
The newspaper is folded in four. The crossword faces up.
I have finished the crossword. Now I shall admire it.
Odile says my reading glasses suit me. I wear them always now.
The kiosk radio plays a waltz. Even the palm trees sway.
Seventeen across: "cypress". The tree is right there. Merci.
I nod to everyone who passes. It is my afternoon profession.
The cat yawned. Then I yawned. It is contagious, you know.
Arm in arm, and a cane for style. Mostly for style.
We walk to the third lamp post and back. A grand tour.
Bonjour, Biscuit. Yes, yes. You are a very fine dog.
The cat is on the wall again. Bonjour, Clémentine.
A gull walks beside us. He keeps our pace, very civil.
I tap the cane on the cobbles. One, two. Like a metronome.
Someone is practising piano behind those shutters. Debussy.
We stop at every bench. Not to sit. To say hello.
Odile notices the flowers. I notice Odile noticing.
Slowly past the fountain. Léo will want to show us a coin.
I know every tile on this promenade. Old friends, all.
We pass the café. Marcel waves the tea towel. We wave back.
The lemon trees look well. I may take some of the credit.
The afternoon smells of salt and warm bread. Perfect.
Biscuit has chosen a different route. We shall follow.
A painter is sketching the zinc roofs. He has the grey right.
Seventy-something steps to the kiosk. I stopped counting.
One loop after the watering, one before supper. Every day.
The cat followed us for six steps. Then she remembered herself.
Four o'clock. The sun moves over to the café side.
A good afternoon has a lemon, a book and a little shade.
The gulls are quieter after lunch. Even they take a siesta.
I keep a biscuit for Biscuit. Yusuf pretends not to see.
My hat has been to every afternoon of this promenade. Faithful.
Odile hums when she is happy. She hums most afternoons.
Somewhere a radio plays Piaf. The whole street listens.
The cat on the wall is orange. I call her Clémentine.
Forty years of afternoons, and I still like this one best.
Camille waved from the steps. Such a kind face.
Théo has a baguette under each arm. A man of ambition.
I mend my own watch strap. Leather, a needle, an afternoon.
The shadows are long enough now to count the cypresses.
I used to play the clarinet. Now I hum. Same tunes, quieter.
Marcel has put out the little blue cups. Tea time, I think.
Léo asked the lemons' age. Older than him, younger than me.
The gull on the lamp post has been there an hour. Professional.
A little more for you. You had the sun all morning.
Thank you for the shade, old tree. Here is your tea.
The breeze helps. It carries the water to the far leaves.
Second can. The geraniums asked very nicely.
You are greener than yesterday. I noticed. Well done.
Warm soil, cool water. Every plant's favourite moment.
Madame Basil, your neighbour is jealous. One splash each.
Three new blossoms this week. I counted them twice.
The rosemary smells of July. Merci, rosemary.
I water. The bees supervise. A fair arrangement.
This pot was Odile's idea. It was a very good idea.
A drop for the pavement too. It works hard all day.
Hold still, little lemon. You are growing beautifully.
The can is light, the afternoon is long. Perfect.
Water first, then the bench. The order of things.
The jasmine is opening. It waits for the warm part of the day.
Marcel filled my can at the café tap. A true gentleman.
The oleander leans toward me. I take it as a greeting.
Every leaf a little bow. I bow back, carefully.
This one I planted the year we married. Still here. Still green.
There. Now you can have your afternoon nap.
The palm does not need me. I water it out of friendship.
Sun on the back of the neck. The best kind of hat weather.
A splash for the cypress. It stands up straight for us all.
Odile says I talk to the lemons. I say they listen.
The fountain and I. Two old men, keeping things wet.
Look, a ladybird. She has chosen the best lemon tree.
You were thirsty. I could tell. No need to say anything.
Odile, your shoulder has sun on it. It suits you.
The breeze turns the newspaper for me. Very helpful.
Seventeen across: "to linger". Five letters. Dally. Yes.
I saved you the shady half, ma chérie. As promised.
The crossword and the afternoon. Both nearly finished, both lovely.
A pencil, a breeze, a wife who knows all the long words.
Monsieur, you dropped your glove. There. Bonne journée.
Lucie waved. I waved. The gull waved, more or less.
The kiosk has new postcards. Odile wants all of them.
Three down: "warm wind". Odile says breeze. Odile is right.
From here I can see four lemon trees. All of them happy.
It is a fine afternoon when the pencil needs sharpening twice.
The shadows are getting longer. So is my crossword.
Odile has fallen asleep on my shoulder. I shall not move.
A child laughed at the fountain. The best sound in town.
Thank you, Marcel. A glass of water, exactly what I wanted.
This bench was painted in spring. It still smells of it.
The warm stone, the cool shade. A bench with both is rare.
Eight letters, "contented". I believe I am the answer.
Your hat is crooked, Odile. There. Magnifique.
Look how slowly the clouds go. Like us, but taller.
A bee on the newspaper. He is reading the weather.
Léo told me a joke. I laughed at the right moment, mostly.
I have been sitting since half past four. A good record.
Odile is counting the white houses. I am counting her smiles.
The lemon scent reaches the bench at exactly this hour.
Seven letters, "gracious". Odile wrote it before I read it.
Our neighbour brought figs. A gift is the best fruit.
Close your eyes. Hear the fountain? It is reciting.
Arm in arm, the long way. There is no short way here.
Mind the step, ma chérie. There. Light as a feather.
Bonjour, madame. Your dog has a magnificent tail.
The cane is mostly for pointing at nice things.
See the whitewash? Someone painted that house this week.
Odile walks faster in the afternoon. I follow, gladly.
Afternoon sun on the promenade. Like walking on honey.
That cypress was a twig when we moved here. Look at him.
Good afternoon, Théo. That is a very handsome loaf.
We pause for the bougainvillea. It deserves an audience.
The palms are whispering. Pleasant gossip, I am sure.
One lap, then another. The promenade is generous.
A bow to the kiosk, a nod to the fountain. Old friends.
Camille, your flowers are splendid. Odile says so too.
The breeze keeps lifting my hat. It wants to see too.
We walk at the speed of the afternoon. Exactly right.
Léo, you have grown a centimetre since Tuesday. Remarkable.
The café chairs are all facing the sea. Very sensible chairs.
Odile, you choose the turn. You always choose well.
Shade, then sun, then shade. Like a slow chessboard.
Afternoon is the lemon's favourite hour. Mine also.
A kind word costs nothing and the shop is always open.
The warmth has settled into the stones. Lovely to the feet.
Everyone is in a good mood. I suspect it is the light.
Lucie rang her bell for me. I tipped my hat for her.
Half past three. The best half of the afternoon begins.
Odile says I am a romantic. Forty-one years of evidence.
A small favour each day. Today: a lost ball returned.
Léo asked to help. Now the path is watered too. Splendid.
A little boy asked if lemons can swim. I said only in tea.
Second round. The trees pretend they have forgotten the first.
This lemon is the size of a walnut. In a month, a fist.
The children run past. The leaves wave after them.
Half a can for the little one by the door. He is shy.
The can is lighter in the afternoon. Or I am stronger.
Look at this one, all blossom. Showing off, I think.
Seventeen pots. I know each of them by first name.
The soil drinks it up. A sound like a small applause.
Léo says the lemons are tall now. Taller than him? Not yet.
The fountain sends a little mist. The basil says merci.
Rosemary, then lemons, then the geraniums. Always that order.
If you listen, the leaves are humming. Or that is the café.
The shadows grow long. A long drink for everyone, then.
I water the trees, the trees give lemons, Odile makes tarte.
The window boxes upstairs wait their turn. Patient creatures.
Careful steps. The cobbles are wet and so am I, a little.
The children at the fountain. Best theatre in town, and free.
Léo is counting coins again. I believe he invents some.
One fills the bucket, the other empties it. A fine system.
A boy just bowed to a pigeon. The pigeon bowed back.
The crossword can wait. The children have started a parade.
Eight down: "happiness", three letters. Joy. Too easy today.
Fifteen across: "evening light", four letters. Lamp.
The pen is in my pocket. The word is on my tongue. Wait.
Odile has the answer. She is letting me find it. Kindly.
Odile beside me, the sun on my hat. Nothing to add.
Sit a while. The afternoon is long and the bench is wide.
I count my blessings on this bench. I run out of fingers.
The paper is folded, the crossword is done. Now we watch.
Soon the lamps. I like to see the very first one.
The café windows are polished. Marcel expects a fine evening.
Somebody is practising piano upstairs. Scales. Lovely scales.
Look, the sun found that window. It glows like a lantern.
The kiosk man waves. I wave the newspaper. We are old friends.
A child gave me a pebble. I shall keep it in my good pocket.
I nod off for a moment. Odile says it was an hour. A good hour.
This bench has held me through four decades. It deserves a medal.
The fountain sings. The children sing louder. A duet.
The light turns honey. The white houses go gold first.
We share the bench with a sparrow. He pays in songs.
Léo is a horse now. A fast horse. It is lap six, he says.
Lucie rang her bell at us. Odile rang her bracelet back.
A boy is wishing on a coin. Whatever it is, I hope yes.
Thank you, sun. Thank you, bench. Thank you, Odile.
A gentle pace. The promenade has been waiting all day for us.
We pass the fountain. Léo salutes. I salute back. Correct.
Arm in arm past the café. Marcel pretends not to watch.
The cane goes tap, the fountain goes splash. A little song.
There is the window where Odile first waved at me. Still there.
Step, step, pause for the view. Step, step, pause again.
The palms lean in to listen. We say nothing of importance.
The kiosk has the evening paper already. Good man.
A stroll is not for going somewhere. It is for being here.
We stop at every planter. Odile says I am inspecting. I am.
Shutters opening for the evening. The town is waking up again.
Soon the café lights. We will be just in time, as always.
The cypresses stand like waiters. Very tall, very polite.
A boy offered me his ice cream. A gentleman declines. Barely.
Slowly, chérie. The sea is not in a hurry, and neither are we.
Look at the zinc roofs. Silver in the afternoon. Like my hair.
The best part of a walk is the bench at the end of it.
Someone has chalked a hopscotch. I did one square. Bravo, me.
An afternoon like this, one says thank you to no one in particular.
Léo has a new bucket. It is red. He told me three times.
The children are at the fountain. All is well in the world.
I have everything I need, and a lemon tree besides.
Four o'clock. The best hour for doing very little.
The light comes in sideways now. Everything looks painted.
One more lemon this week. I count them like grandchildren.
Upstairs a kettle whistles. Tea time somewhere, very good.
My hat, my cane, my Odile. All an afternoon requires.
A tea towel drying on a balcony. Even laundry looks happy here.
When the fountain catches the sun, it throws little rainbows.
The church bell says five. The café cups agree.
A child laughed so hard he sat down. That is the best kind.
Afternoon is the good chair of the day. Sit in it.
At my age, a calm afternoon is a great achievement.
Henri, you are a lucky man, I tell myself. Daily. Correctly.
Patience, children. The ice cream man knows where you are.
All these years, and still a little thrill at the first lamp.
Bonjour, madame. A fine afternoon to be walking slowly.
Ah, monsieur. Your hat is excellent. I notice these things.
Do you hear that? Marcel is stacking saucers. Like small bells.
The bakery smells of the second batch. Lucie will know already.
Afternoon, little one. Is that a new ice cream? Lemon, I hope.
I wonder who painted the kiosk that shade of green. Good choice.
Bonjour again. Twice in one day. We are practically cousins.
The fountain is chattering to itself. It has a lot to say today.
Smell that? Somebody is frying garlic. A wise household.
How does Léo run so fast? I walked that fast once. In 1974.
The cypresses smell warm. Like a pencil sharpened in the sun.
A little breeze, a little shade. Exactly the right amounts.
Good afternoon. No, no hurry. There is never a hurry here.
I hear Odile laughing from three benches away. A fine sound.
Is it Thursday? It feels like a Thursday. Very agreeable.
Somebody is shaking out a tablecloth. Crumbs for the sparrows.
Bonjour, Théo. Working hard? Ah. Good. Neither am I.
Where do the swallows go at four o'clock? Somewhere important.
The string lights are asleep. They will wake at dusk, like owls.
Ah, the church bell. Half past four. I counted every one.
Fresh paint on the railing. Someone has been thoughtful.
A child is whistling. Badly. With tremendous confidence.
Coffee from the café and jasmine from the wall. A fine duet.
I wonder what the gulls talk about. Lunch, mostly, I expect.
Monsieur, you look lost in the nicest way. The sea is that way.
Camille, bonjour. Léo is a comet today. We all saw.
The zinc roofs ticking in the warmth. They do that, you know.
Bonjour. Yes, everyone says bonjour here. It is the law of joy.
Hm. Oranges or lemons, from that balcony? I must investigate.
There goes Lucie's bell. Ding ding. Like a punctuation mark.
One small cloud, very well behaved. Good afternoon, cloud.
Good afternoon. I recommend the shade under the second palm.
Is that rosemary? Somebody brushed past it. Lovely.
Afternoon round. Good afternoon, lemons. Thirsty again?
Wet earth and lemon leaves. I would bottle it if I could.
Bonjour, little bud. I see you. Take your time.
The can sings a different note when it is nearly empty.
Lemon number nine is the shy one. Always behind a leaf.
How do they grow so round? I have asked. They keep quiet.
Slowly. A good watering is a conversation, not a speech.
Ah, the basil. I brushed it. Now the whole step smells Italian.
A drop on the leaf makes a tiny lens. Look, a little sun.
The pots are warm as bread. Time for a long cool drink.
Fill, pour, admire. Fill, pour, admire. A perfect routine.
Smell the soil? That is the smell of next week's lemons.
One for the lemons, a splash for the sparrow bath. Fair is fair.
The jasmine wants attention too. Very well, madame.
Is this lemon bigger than yesterday? I believe it is. Bravo.
Good afternoon, passer-by. Mind the puddle. It is a happy one.
Ah, the bench is warm. It has been waiting for me all day.
Good afternoon. Sit, sit. There is room for three crosswords.
From this bench you can hear the whole town hum. Listen.
Spoons on saucers, a bicycle bell, gulls. The afternoon choir.
Seven letters, "to stroll". Saunter. Merci, Odile.
I wonder how many people have sat on this bench. Thousands. Good.
The paper is warm from the sun. Straight to the crossword.
Monsieur, bonjour. The view is free. Take as much as you like.
Do you suppose the pigeons have a bench of their own?
A pencil, a paper, a bench. All the technology I need.
The palm leaves rustle like someone turning pages.
Hm, "sea breeze", five letters. Wait, I can smell the answer.
Léo, how many laps is that? He says eleven. He means four.
Bonjour, little dog. Yes, I have a biscuit. No, not for you.
The afternoon sun, on the left knee only. Exquisite.
The lavender pots behind us. Every breeze, a small present.
Good afternoon, neighbour. Yes, the good bench. As always.
Listen. Marcel is humming in the doorway again. Puccini.
Smell the sea air? It cleans the thoughts. Very efficient.
Is the kiosk selling peaches today? I smell peaches.
Bonjour, mademoiselle. Yes, we are the slowest. It is a choice.
I wonder who lives behind the blue shutters. Musical people.
We walk to the end and back. The end is always delighted.
Hear that? The fountain splashing and children counting.
Odile, have you noticed? The café smells of almond today.
Bonjour, Marcel! No coffee, merci. We are only admiring.
Shall we stop at the railing? The blue is extra blue today.
Grafting a lemon branch. Lesson three. Very delicate work.
Léo taught me to whistle with two fingers. The lemons were startled.
I am practising my Italian on the basil. It is very forgiving.
The day the first lemon tree arrived, Odile wore her yellow dress.
I read a book on soil. Now I say "loam" with great authority.
My first harvest here: three lemons. We made one very small tarte.
Patience. The lemons are excellent teachers of it.
Citrus limon, the Latin name. It sounds like a duke.
This pot came from the summer market the year the lights went up.
Odile is teaching me to pinch the basil tops. Snip. Like so.
I have learned to pour with my left hand too. Ambidextrous at last.
Léo once watered my shoes instead. We both laughed for an hour.
Keeping a notebook now. Tuesday: two blossoms, one bee, one smile.
A new knot for the stake. Look how proudly the tree stands.
First spring here, I watered the plastic flowers next door. Twice.
Learning to tell lemons by weight. This one: nearly ready. Heavy.
I am practising a little song for each pot. The jasmine gets a waltz.
The rain barrel was a birthday gift from Théo. A thoughtful man.
My first can leaked like a sieve. I loved it anyway. Twelve years.
Odile and I planted the rosemary on a Sunday. It still smells of it.
I am learning to prune by eye, not by ruler. Very modern of me.
Camille drew my lemon tree once. It hangs above our stove.
I have learned the word "compost" in four languages. All lovely.
Marcel and I once carried this big pot together. Very theatrical.
Learning which leaf is new: lighter green, softer. Like a baby's ear.
The summer of the great lemonade stand. Léo sold eleven cups.
Odile is teaching me to knit. I have made one long, brave stripe.
I am memorising a Prévert poem. Two verses down, three to go.
Practising card tricks for Léo. The queen keeps escaping.
I am learning to sketch. The fountain looks like a teapot, mostly.
Practising my chess openings. The pigeon is a weak opponent.
Learning the names of clouds. That one is cumulus. Fluffy fellow.
Remember the night the whole promenade danced? I wore two hats.
I am learning bird calls. Swallow, sparrow, gull. Gull is easiest.
Odile is teaching me her tarte recipe. I may write it in ink.
Practising the harmonica. Very softly. The cat approves, I think.
I learned five new crossword words this week. Today: "halcyon".
Here we shared our first ice cream in town. Pistachio, both.
I am learning to sit without the newspaper. Hands free. Strange.
Léo is teaching me football words. A "nutmeg" is not a spice.
The day Marcel started at the café, he dropped one cup. Just one.
Learning to draw hands. Mine look like friendly lettuces.
Practising my handwriting. Odile says I loop my l's beautifully.
The year the fountain was restored, we sat here every day to watch.
I am learning watercolour. Everything turns lovely and a bit blue.
Camille brought baby Léo past this bench first. He held my finger.
Learning a new patience game. I am patient. The cards less so.
The first evening of the string lights, everyone clapped. Me too.
I am learning the names of every house. That one is Les Mimosas.
We walked this route on our very first day here. Same tiles.
Practising my bow. Low, slow, a little flourish. Like so.
I am learning to walk without the cane on Sundays. Short Sundays.
Lucie is teaching me bicycle signals. Left arm out. Very official.
I count the cypresses in Italian now. Uno, due, tre. Practising.
Here is where I found Odile's lost earring. Shining in the sun.
Léo taught me the names of six beetles. I greet them all now.
Remember the year it snowed here, chérie? One flake each. Magic.
Practising my posture. Odile taps my back. Up, Henri. Like a palm.
I am learning the old songs from the kiosk radio. Verse two, today.
We are learning a new route. Left at the fountain. Very daring.
Our tenth anniversary, we walked here at dusk. Still my favourite.
I have learned to walk and admire at the same time. Late talent.
Here the children once made a chalk map of the whole town. Huge.
Odile is teaching me to spot a good fig from three steps away.
Learning the shortcut through the lavender. Short, but fragrant.
We met Camille and Théo here, the week they moved in. Such joy.
I am learning to make limoncello. Odile is my official taster.
At my age, learning something new each day keeps the hat on straight.
Practising my juggling with three lemons. Two is going very well.
The first summer we lived here, we ate lemons with everything.
I learned to tie a bow tie this week. For no reason. Just joy.
Remember Marcel's first café opera night? He sang the whole menu.
A new hobby: pressing flowers. The jasmine flattens very politely.
Learning to cook ratatouille from Marcel. Slowly, he says. Like you.
The happiest afternoon: Odile's laugh when the lemon tree bloomed.
I am practising a toast for Sunday dinner. Short. Very short.
Lucie's first bicycle had a basket of daisies. She rang it all day.
I learned to skip a stone once. Now I teach Léo. He does five.
The day this bench arrived, I sat on it first. A small honour.
I am practising my aim. Right at the roots. Bullseye, little tree.
Learning to read the leaves. Curled means thirsty. Flat means happy.
Practising my poem aloud. A gull stopped to listen. Encouraging.
Odile is teaching me to spot the first star. A little early yet.
The afternoon Léo learned to ride a bike, right there. Huge cheers.
I am learning the dance Marcel does with his tray. Mostly the spin.
Practising my stride. Odile says I walk like a dignified heron.
I am learning to bake bread. My first loaf was a cheerful brick.
Remember the lantern parade? Léo carried a lemon-shaped lantern.
The lemons have gone to bed. I can tell. They fold up a little.
Blue hour. The bougainvillea turns the colour of a good plum.
Tomorrow, the third lemon tree gets a new pot. A terracotta one.
My mother kept geraniums on every sill. I keep lemons. Progress.
From this bench I can count my lemon trees. Four. All present.
Odile says the jasmine smells strongest now. She is right again.
The jasmine opens at dusk. A late riser, like my brother Paul.
Look how the lamps come on. Like lemons ripening, one by one.
Plans for tomorrow: water, paper, café, Odile. In that order.
Tomorrow I prune the bougainvillea. Gently. It has opinions.
The pink one by the kiosk climbed a whole hand today. Bravo.
I planted that cypress the year Odile said yes. Look at it now.
Our first evening here, we sat on this very bench. Same paint.
A bench, a blue sky going dark, a wife beside me. Enough.
The rosemary by the steps wants trimming. Thursday, I think.
My grandson writes that his basil is doing well. Takes after me.
The geraniums on Camille's balcony. Red as a postman's van.
Every window lit is someone home for supper. I like that.
Odile is naming the stars. She makes up half of them. Lovely.
The palm by the fountain is older than me. Barely.
Seven-thirty tomorrow, the market. I want the knobbly lemons.
When I was a boy, my father grew tomatoes on a tin roof.
Odile's sister sends a postcard every June. Always lavender.
Just sit. The flowers do the rest of the work at this hour.
The string lights are on. The oleander looks very dressed up.
Hm. The lemon on the left is nearly ready. Saturday, perhaps.
We courted on a bench like this. I had more hair. Same hat.
A note for tomorrow: buy twine for the climbing rose.
This evening the sea is the colour of Odile's good scarf.
Our daughter rang. The children are planting sunflowers.
Look, the bougainvillea is still pink in the dark. Stubborn.
The swifts have gone to bed. The lamps take the next shift.
I told the lemon trees about the crossword. They were impressed.
Soon, Marcel will light the candles. Then, a small glass.
After this, the café. After the café, the stairs. A full plan.
Forty-one summers of jasmine on this promenade. Still new.
The fig by the church gate is heavy this year. Jam in a week.
Odile's mother taught her to press flowers. She still does.
In the morning, I will thank the lemons for the shade.
The blue hour is very short. One must not talk through it.
Hush. The lamp by the café is about to come on. There.
Our wedding day, the bougainvillea was in bloom. It remembers.
My knees and the lemon trees agree: a cool evening is best.
That little olive by the post office. I gave it a name. Gaston.
Gaston the olive has three new leaves. A good week for Gaston.
Next spring, a lemon for the kiosk. I have asked nicely.
I keep a notebook of every lemon. Two hundred and six so far.
Odile and I will walk the long way home. The jasmine way.
Our son climbed that palm once. Halfway. Then he sat and waved.
The lavender pots are asleep. Their smell stays up late.
